https://www.bursa.ro/lapar-transit-of-uk.text: The League of Agricultural Producers Associations of Romania (LAPAR) demands full traceability, firm controls and priority for Romanian goods in the transport infrastructure and port operations. Farmers in our country are asking the authorities to implement a strict control mechanism for Ukrainian grains in transit, amid information regarding the possible reactivation of solidarity corridors. The employers' federation warns that a repeat of the situation in 2022-2023 could put pressure on Romanian farmers and the national logistics infrastructure again. "Agriculture needs a miracle or at least a series of common sense measures to deal with the problems associated with the transit of Ukrainian cereals on Romanian territory. Taking into account the recent memory of what happened in 2022-2023, corroborated with the fact that we hear in the public space about the possibility of reopening the solidarity corridors, I want to sound an alarm: this can generate very large disproportions in the market, with negative effects on the agricultural sector and logistics," said Matei Titianu, president of LAPAR, during a press conference held yesterday at the headquarters of IMM Romania. In a document sent to the authorities in our country, LAPAR proposes to approve each transport before entering Romania, regardless of whether it comes directly from Ukraine or through the Republic of Moldova. The approval would indicate the cargo, the mode of transport and the border crossing point, and the data would be reported at three-day intervals. Farmers also demand the mandatory correlation of entry and exit documents, so that the entire quantity declared in transit can be tracked until it leaves the national territory. "We need rigorous control and full traceability of agricultural products from Ukraine on Romanian territory. We do not want the origins to be washed away again, so that Ukrainian products are sold as Moldovan cereals or Romanian cereals. We need prior approval of flows; at the time of entry into Romania, we need an approval that precisely specifies the crossing point, the goods and the transit mode. We need the approvals at entry to coincide with those at exit from the country. We need the prioritization of Romanian goods by rail, through a transparent mechanism, protected from commercial interference", stated Matei Titianu. The list of requested measures also includes the activation of warehouses on Romanian territory, the use of predefined routes monitored by CNAIR and the Romanian Police, dedicated transfer lines and weighing of transport at all border points, including the border with the Republic of Moldova. For rail transport, LAPAR requests the verification of the seals of the loading and unloading gates. "We need to know how transport and the quantities transiting the Romanian state are monitored. In 2022-2023, access to the port of Constanţa was very difficult, and farmers waited for days. Romania's infrastructure must be seen as critical infrastructure. Therefore, we request the establishment of a real consultation framework before adopting new measures regarding solidarity corridors," said the LAPAR president. He recalled that the pressure on transport infrastructure is amplified by the low level of the Danube, the overloading of the road network and the increase in energy and road and rail transport costs. Under these conditions, LAPAR believes that transit must be organized through clear rules, effective controls and verifiable traceability mechanisms, in order not to restrict the real access of Romanian products to the market. https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/andrew-tate-lu.text: Andrew Tate's carefully cultivated image of extreme wealth has come under fresh scrutiny after court documents reportedly revealed that several of the luxury cars repeatedly featured in content associated with the Tate brothers were rented rather than owned.Documents submitted during Andrew and Tristan Tate's ongoing legal battle reportedly state that a $2.1 million (£1.5 million) Aston Martin and two Bugattis valued at $5 million (£4 million) and $7 million (£5 million) were rented. The revelation has reignited debate over the influencer's long-running social media persona, which has frequently centred on expensive cars, private jets and displays of extravagant wealth.Tate Brothers' Luxury Cars Were Reportedly RentedAccording to court documents, the Tate brothers' lawyers specifically addressed claims about their wealth while arguing that the pair should not be considered a flight risk because of supposedly vast financial resources. The filing reportedly stated that the $2.1 million Aston Martin and the $5 million and $7 million Bugattis featured in Tristan Tate's videos were rented.The disclosure is particularly notable because luxury vehicles have long played an important role in the brothers' online branding. Andrew Tate famously used the Bugatti as a symbol of success, even turning the phrase 'What colour is your Bugatti?' into a recurring taunt aimed at critics.Earlier reporting has also documented Tate's association with an extensive collection of luxury vehicles. Romanian authorities seized a fleet of cars linked to the brothers in 2023, including an Aston Martin, Ferrari, Porsche, BMW, Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Benz.The Cars Helped Build Tate's Online ImageFor years, Tate has presented himself as an example of the wealth and lifestyle his followers could supposedly achieve.His social media videos have frequently featured supercars, expensive watches, private aircraft and other symbols of financial success. His online businesses have also been built around teaching customers how to make money.The newly reported court filing appears to acknowledge that projecting wealth was part of the brothers' business strategy.According to court documents, the Tates have businesses centred on 'teaching' men how to earn money and therefore have an interest in portraying themselves online as exceptionally wealthy.That admission has prompted renewed questions about how much of the lifestyle presented in their videos represented actual ownership and how much was designed as marketing.What About Tate's Other Wealth Claims?The revelation about the cars does not, by itself, prove that Tate lacks wealth or that every luxury item he has displayed was rented.Court documents reportedly challenge specific claims made about the brothers' assets, arguing that government allegations relied heavily on social media posts and claims about their lifestyle rather than definitive proof of ownership.The filing also reportedly addressed a $50 million (£37 million) superyacht associated with the brothers, claiming that it did not belong to them and that they had instead been paid to promote it on social media.The distinction lies between saying Tate has no money and recognising that some of the wealth displayed online was not actually his.Tate's Bugatti Became a Symbol of His PersonaThe Bugatti was more than just another expensive vehicle in Tate's content. It became one of the most recognisable symbols of his online identity.Research into Tate's influence has previously noted how phrases such as 'What colour is your Bugatti?' became associated with his brand and were used by followers as a shorthand for status and success.The revelation that some of the Bugattis featured in the brothers' videos were rented has created an ironic twist to one of Tate's most recognisable boasts.It also raises broader questions about influencer culture, where luxury cars, designer watches and exotic holidays can be used not only as personal possessions but as carefully selected props for building an online image.For Tate, whose business model has relied heavily on presenting himself as the ultimate example of male success, the reported court admission could prove particularly damaging to the authenticity of that persona.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/17/euro.text: At one of the biggest financial forums in Central Asia, Euronews moderated a panel focusing on Kazakhstan drive to turn its position at the heart of Eurasia into more than a transit advantage, by developing logistics, manufacturing and investment.Infrastructure investor Nurzhan Marabayev said efficient, transparent and competitive logistics could unlock new projects across Central Asia. Kazakhstan has relatively low labour, resource and construction costs, he noted, but expensive logistics remain a challenge for the landlocked country.Airport director Meruyert Zholdybayeva highlighted the potential of multimodal transport, citing a China-Europe route that moves goods from Shenzhen to Europe in seven days. She said Aktau could eventually become a major hub combining rail, sea and air links.Manufacturing is also expanding. Alima Issembayeva said production rose from 2.3 trillion tenge in 2021 to almost 4 trillion in 2025, while exports more than doubled between 2021 and 2024.Trade expert Ilya Urazakov cited Kazakhstan’s FDI record and natural resources as key advantages, while Professor Tom Vinaimont stressed the need for currency hedging and predictable financing.

https://www.politico.eu/article/mark-car.text: Earlier this year, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered some avuncular counsel to Western allies at Davos, weary of being belittled and trolled by President Donald Trump and his advisers: “Sit back, take a deep breath, do not retaliate,” he urged. “Let things play out.” His remarks focused primarily on tariffs, but at the Swiss Alpine gabfest, Bessent and other Trump aides repeated the same advice on almost everything concerning the U.S. president. And on the whole, the leaders of Washington’s allies heeded their warning, even as they struggled to contain their outrage over Trump’s threats to invade Greenland. For Gavin Newsom, the Trump-bashing California governor who was also at Davos, it was all too much . The world leaders in attendance were “pathetic,” he said. “I can’t take this complicity of people rolling over. I should have brought a bunch of knee pads for all the world leaders.” Advertisement Advertisement Since then, however, things have moved on — especially for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron, who have both been giving as good as they get in recent weeks. Amid rising trade tensions and differences with the White House over Russia, they haven’t hesitated to escalate when attacked, sometimes even taunting Trump without immediate provocation. Carney and Macron have become the “leaders of the resistance,” said Rohinton Medhora, the Canadian economist and professor at McGill University who has dubbed Carney’s evolving political vision as “value-based realism.” Medhora, who sits on various international and Canadian commissions, said: “They’ve tried flattery. They’ve tried ignoring him. Nothing’s worked, and they are not losing out now with their retaliatory trolling.” Carney may have lectured the Trump administration “to stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough,” but that hasn’t stopped him from offering public mockery of his own. The Canadian prime minister’s freewheeling swipes have included teasing Trump for claiming “sabotage” after his teleprompter malfunctioned during an address to the United Nations last year. Experiencing a similar technical hiccup in Toronto, Carney deadpanned: “I would now like to inform you that the teleprompter has ceased to function. Unlike a certain world leader, I do not view this as a conspiracy.” And in Ottawa, Carney drew both applause and laughter by mimicking Trump’s signature “accordion” hand gestures . So, what’s going on? And are there any risks to poking the bear? Advertisement Advertisement According to former White House strategist and current MAGA influencer and podcaster Steve Bannon, there is. “They’re playing with fire,” he told POLITICO. “They’re totally dependent on us for trade.” He also added a dark warning about “the Alberta secession movement picking up momentum” — Bannon and other MAGA luminaries have been encouraging the oil-rich Canadian province to break away. Bannon also cited the deal Trump recently struck with Denmark and Greenland as an example of U.S. power and Washington’s ability to get what it wants. “Our Greenland deal shows the reality of Canada’s inability to defend itself from being the next Ukraine — this time in the Arctic,” he said. But Ivo Daalder, a former U.S. ambassador to NATO, draws a different lesson from the Greenland deal, which extends an earlier agreement dating from 1951 and does not give Trump control of the island, as he said he wanted. For Daalder, this deal shows that when allies stand their ground, the U.S. president backs down. “With that deal Trump literally got nothing,” he told POLITICO. Donald Trump, Macron and Carney attend a working lunch during the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Evelyn Hockstein via Getty Images “I think what’s happening is the allies are starting to understand how to play him,” said Daalder. “Now they’re ignoring his bluster, and do and say what they think is important for their own good. By doing so, they have as good a chance as any in getting what they want.” It’s also not surprising that Macron was quicker to taunt Trump than other Western leaders, said Daalder. “He’s French, after all.” Even during the first Trump presidency, Macron was willing to go mano a mano with the U.S. president, squeezing his counterpart’s hand in a handshake until their knuckles turned white and refusing to let go even when Trump tried to pull away. But the French president’s tone seems sharper now, his actions even more pointed. Fort his, Daalder points to Macron’s maneuvering of Trump this June into inking an interim deal with Iran at Versailles — a palace infamous for a treaty that ended one world war but led to another. Macron, Trump’s critics trumpeted, had pulled off an epic diplomatic “troll.” Advertisement Advertisement What audiences are these two leaders trying to reach and influence? “That’s a good question,” said Medhora. “It is clearly not Americans.” And there’s certainly a domestic component, as both men are scoring political points by standing up to a man they portray as a bully. But Medhora believes there is likely a broader, more strategic, aspect to their posturing. “By doing these things very publicly, they’re encouraging other leaders to overcome their hesitation and join them,” he said. “And if others come along, then everyone is stronger in the anti-Trump camp.” But that’ll only work if they can do it with serious consequence — and there’s always a chance that it could all backfire. Perhaps with Trump facing a likely setback in the U.S. midterm elections, Carney and Macron would be better off taking Bessent’s advice and letting things play out, as the U.S. leader may emerge from the vote facing new constraints from emboldened Democrats. But, for now, both seem to be having far too much fun poking the bear to do that.

https://bnn-news.com/world/french-presid.text: Raphaël Glucksmann · Photo: PES/Flickr Advertisements Raphaël Glucksmann, a center-left candidate for the French presidency, has condemned US President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, Politico reports. Speaking at the Politico Competitiveness Summit in Paris, Glucksmann stated that the US is led by a man who is either a "useful idiot" or is deliberately seeking to destroy Europe's strength and freedom. He emphasized that Russia's war in Ukraine directly affects Europeans. Glucksmann insisted that a victory for his rival, far-right politician Marine Le Pen, in the 2027 presidential election would also be a victory for Russian dictator Putin and a step closer to Europe's defeat. Le Pen has previously expressed a degree of admiration for Putin, and her party, the National Rally (RN), received a loan in 2014 from a bank linked to Russia. Le Pen explained that the party borrowed abroad because no French bank would grant it a loan, and maintained that the loan did not influence her political stance in any way. The party has since repaid the loan. Advertisements Although Le Pen has condemned Moscow's war in Ukraine, several elected officials from her party strongly oppose support for Ukraine and favor closer ties with Russia. At a Politico event in September, Le Pen stated that while France could assist Ukraine with military training and support, it would no longer be able to provide financial aid due to budget constraints. Le Pen has currently emerged as the clear frontrunner in the race for the presidency. Glucksmann, one of the most pro-European candidates for the upcoming elections, reiterated in an interview with *Politico* his support for the European Sky Shield project and the need to build a more unified, sovereign European defense industry. This initiative is also backed by current French President Emmanuel Macron and a large number of French politicians. Glucksmann remarked that for decades, Europe had entrusted its security and sovereignty to Washington, and there is now a growing realization of how misguided that choice was. The politician stated that without joint investment, no European nation—including Germany—would be capable of confronting future warfare, describing it as a "matter of life and death." In an interview, Glucksmann outlined what his foreign policy would look like should he succeed in assuming the presidency in 2027: it would focus on strengthening relations between European nations rather than attempting to appease leaders such as Putin or Chinese President Xi Jinping. He stated that he would prefer to visit Warsaw or Tallinn over Beijing or Moscow. Glucksmann has frequently criticized the lavish reception accorded to Putin at the Palace of Versailles in 2017, as well as Macron’s decision to take Xi on a tour of the French president's grandmother's native village in southwestern France. Advertisements The center-left candidate argued that Europe needs to balance the power dynamic in negotiations with China. He also maintained that the European Union should stick to its goal of phasing out the production of internal combustion engine vehicles by 2035 and invest more heavily in electric vehicle manufacturing to avoid ceding the entire sector to China. Glucksmann presents himself as a French president who would stand up to figures viewed as leaders of global superpowers—such as Xi, Putin, and Trump. Meanwhile, as the election campaign gains momentum, Glucksmann is also seeking to strengthen his position on domestic policy issues. He stated that the student protests—which, among other issues, have arisen due to teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and dilapidated schools—are entirely legitimate and justified. Glucksmann also pointed out that teachers' salaries are too low.
